item.title: What Personality Reveals About Musical Choices
item.description:
Personality

What Personality Reveals About Musical Choices

Patterns in what we listen to reveal aspects of who we are.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Personality predicts musical preference better than age, education, or gender.
  • Major and minor chords activate different brain circuits linked to emotion and processing.
  • Extroverts often prefer stimulating music; introverts lean toward calm, relaxing tunes.
From the Piano Sonata No. 13 (Beethoven) Op. 27, No. 1. in E-flat major (Quasi una fantasia).
Source: Roberto, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Do you prefer music written in a major or a minor key? It turns out this preference might just depend on your personality. So, let’s start at the beginning and look at what personality is.

Defining Personality

The APA defines personality as “the enduring configuration of characteristics and behavior that comprises an individual’s unique adjustment to life, including major traits, interests, drives, values, self-concept, abilities, and emotional patterns.” (American Psychological Association, 2018). We can see personality in any number of things we do, from whether or not we like spicy food to the characteristics we seek in a partner, and even a preference for music in a particular key.

Hans and Sylvia Eysenck proposed a very influential model of personality based on biology and genetics (Psychologists World, 2026). The Eysencks proposed a “trait model” of personality. Traits are stable characteristics of a person, like the way they think or behave, that distinguish that person from everyone else. Traits are often arranged on a continuum from high to low levels of that characteristic at either end. A given individual might show a lot of a trait, or only a little of it. The real question for researchers quickly became how many traits might there be.

The Eysencks proposed what has come to be called PEN theory, suggesting our personalities were composed of three traits:

  • Psychoticism/Normality. Someone characterized by high Psychoticism might be irresponsible, unwilling to accept social norms, and needing gratification without regard to consequences. A low score on this trait would indicate the opposite trends in behavior.
  • Neuroticism/Emotional Stability. Individuals who show high levels of Neuroticism tend to be anxious, they worry a lot about things others would dismiss as minor, and they tend to focus on the negative in life. Personalities at the other end of this continuum tend to be more emotionally stable, to be calmer in a stressful situation, and to be more tolerant of both their own failings and those of others.
  • Extroversion/Introversion. Extroverts tend to be social, outgoing, and at ease in groups, while introverts tend to be quiet, prefer solitude, and often avoid large groups.

Eysenck linked extroversion and introversion to resting levels of cortical arousal. He also proposed that each of us differs in how much cortical stimulation we need or seek out to be comfortable. That level of arousal, termed hedonic tone, is different for each of us. Extroverts tend to have low levels of cortical arousal, which motivates them to seek out stimulation from the environment around them. Introverts, on the other hand, have higher levels of cortical arousal, and so don’t need (and even avoid) stimulation from the external world.

The Big Five model of personality
Source: Eganos, CC BY-SA 4..0 via Wikimedia Commons

A related trait theory, now called the Big Five theory, suggests that personalities are composed of five traits, again arranged on continuums. They are Emotional Stability vs. Instability, Extroversion vs. Introversion, Openness to Experience vs. Conventionality, Agreeableness vs. Antagonism, and Conscientiousness vs. Disinhibition (Widiger and Crego, 2019). Notice the overlap between Eysenck’s three dimensions and the Big Five model. There is a lot of agreement, even amidst the disagreement, about how many traits there might be.

Personality and Musical Preferences

So, back to musical preferences. Greenberg, Kosinski, Stillwell, Monterio, Levitin, and Rentfrow (2016) examined how personality characteristics influenced musical preferences. They wanted to avoid categorizing the musical pieces used in their study according to genre or musical style because of the potential for misunderstanding of these kinds of terms. So, they first asked 76 judges with no formal training in music to rate a large set of snippets of music from a number of genres along a set of 38 dimensions or attributes. These evaluations revealed three essential components: arousal (intense vs gentle or calming), valence (happy vs. sad), and depth (inspiring and poetic vs. danceable, party music).

They then recruited 9,454 volunteers to listen to 50 excerpts of musical pieces and rate their preferences for each piece using the three components of music determined in the first study. They were also asked to take an assessment of their personalities using the Big Five model. They found that personality predicted musical preference over and above demographic measures like age, education, and gender. Interestingly, one characteristic where differences were seen in preference was for the arousing aspects of music. Extroverts tended to prefer music that was stimulating, while introverts tended to prefer relaxing or calm music. Eysenck’s model would predict both of these results.

In a fascinating study of how music affects reward and pleasure in the brain, Suzuki, Okamura et al. (2008) asked volunteers to listen to concordant, discordant, major, and minor chords. Both major and minor concordant chords were rated as beautiful (major chords were rated slightly higher), while discordant major and minor chords were rated as ugly. Major and minor chords also affected quite different circuits in the brain. Minor chords activated brain regions that play an important role in reward and emotion processing, while equally beautiful major chords activated regions associated with orderly and coherent information processing.

In their Arousal Regulation Model of Affective Disorders, Hegerl, Sander & Hensch (2016, Chapter 12) suggest that we often use our own behavior to regulate our neural arousal. Perhaps understanding how music affects our emotional responses and our neural arousal may help clinicians develop more effective ways to use music to treat mood and emotional disorders. It might also shed light on an activity almost all of us find to be pleasurable.

item.title: “Self-Esteem Will Get You Through”
item.description:
Self-Esteem

“Self-Esteem Will Get You Through”

Our kids need a certain type of self for the demands our society places on us.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Self-esteem has become a contentious topic. Some parents and schools are criticized for promoting it.
  • We have become a society of individuals, and this requires that each person be self-determining.
  • To function in this way, we seem to need an early cocoon in which we receive a lot of empathetic attention.

In a previous post—which was itself a follow-up to one on the role of social media as a resource for self-making—I asked if we’re suffering a “narcissism epidemic.” I want to continue here with further thoughts on interpreting our pervasive concern with the self.

If there is a “capital” that parents hope to transmit to their children, it is confidence and lack of trepidation in pursuing opportunities. According to surveys and interviews we have done over the years, parents want their children to see their own life in active not passive, leader not follower, terms. They worry that in decisive moments their child will be inhibited or will, as one father put it, “sell yourself short.” To flourish in this uncertain world, children need to be sure of themselves, to have high self-esteem.

Your “self-esteem,” stated one mother, “that’s what’s going to get you through everything.” Added another, “I build them up and let them know … how special they are.” And that’s important, she said, echoing a common reflection, “Because I had very low self-esteem. I didn’t give myself full advantage in life because I felt that I wasn’t good enough.” For her children, she wants that mental advantage.

Source: Towfiqu barbhuiya/Unsplash

These parents’ positive comments clash with the criticism now commonly leveled against self-esteem and efforts to promote it. In a 2025 book on What Happened to Millennials, for instance, the author, reporter Charlie Wells, charges the self-esteem movement among parents and schools, which first rose to prominence in the 1980s, with inflating “the millennial sense of self.” A whole generation, he observes, was getting trophies just for participating and reciting “you are special” mantras in front of the mirror. So that they would feel less bad about themselves for getting wrong answers, their “teachers stopped using red pens.” Like other detractors, he cites the national campaign to raise self-esteem as a misguided social experiment that has helped produce a lot of fragile, narcissistic people who can’t handle failure.1

The critics are a little fuzzy on why the “obsession with self-esteem” suddenly took hold. Wells faults the blind following of bad science. Research documenting correlation, he claims, got misread as showing causation—feeling bad about yourself doesn’t cause you to do bad things, it results from having done them. Another view comes from a psychologist, who has written extensively on the subject. She suggests that craze began when the “Boomers who now filled the ranks of parents apparently decided that children should always feel good about themselves.”2 Since no reasons are given for this “decision,” the implication is that it was irrational and so was everything that followed.

While there is undoubtedly a lot misguided about the methods people have used to foster self-esteem—critics provide many absurd anecdotes—I don’t think the worry itself is irrational. A high value was placed on self-esteem for a reason. To see it, we have to consider the predicament of the self in contemporary life.

The Society of Individuals

As the critics observe, our society is now awash in talk of self. We all know this, of course. We encounter it everywhere. It permeates our institutions, our popular culture, our media, and, needless to say, our vast consumer and self-improvement industries, which are all about me, my needs, and my body. Practically everything is.

Prizing the self in this way comes at the expense of those realities we reference by “we,” “us,” “ours.” No question of that. But the sheer scope of our focus on the self, our enshrining it as a kind of sacred value, indicates that far more than any individual pathology is at stake. We have become a society of individuals, organized for individuals. This is our condition, our shared way of life, and it requires that each of us operate as a self-determining self, with minimal collective support.

In recent decades, the “individualization” process, as sociologists call it, has accelerated. The older forms of life and culture that regulated human behavior have further eroded or disappeared, enlarging the space of individual freedom and decision-making. While bringing many benefits, greater liberty and more choices leave us to our own devices to make our way in this highly complex and dynamic environment. We are under intensified demands to both regulate and steer ourselves—more decisions and more identity options, increased responsibility to create our own social bonds, new obligations to define our own life purposes, and so on.

What is required of us is not just more knowledge or learned skills but a self—a certain way to be—that can handle the heavy lifting we, as individuals, are now continuously forced to do. Despite what we sometimes hear, we’re not born with this self. We have to acquire it.

Parenting for Self-Esteem

Acquisition, as commonly proposed, involves a paradox. On the one hand, we have the demand to be the kind of masterful self that can function in a highly autonomous way, and has, psychologists and self-help writers often add, the “ability to be self-soothing, self-loving, and self-sufficient.” And, as young people themselves report, the facility to be assertive, confident, flexible, and risk-taking. However, to develop this type of self, and I’m quoting the psychologist Philip Cushman, “many psychologists argue that one must have a nurturing early environment that provides a great deal of empathy, attention, and mirroring.”3

In other words, to get the self-determining self that is now needed in our highly individualized society, we first must be immersed in a social environment that is nearly the exact opposite. Developing autonomy, in this view, requires parents and teachers to provide a protective cocoon in which children receive a lot of empathetic attention.

We don’t have to go very far back in our history to see the radical novelty here. A hundred years ago, for instance, an expert on infant care could write: “The rule that parents should not play with their children may seem hard but it is without doubt a safe one.”4 Rather than a timeless truth of good parenting, high levels of emotional nurturance are better seen as a response to our new situation, as an attempt to provide secure ground on which the necessary self can begin to get some footing.

To be sure, there is a lot of talk of different parenting “styles,” much criticism of “overparenting,” and the backlash against school-based self-esteem efforts. But in none of this, as far as I know, even with so-called “tiger parenting,” is affection, support, and some prioritizing of children’s individualized needs in question. The points of contention, such as how strict to be or how much direction to give, are really just questions of how best to foster the required self.

Perhaps we all know, like the parents we interviewed, that love of self does not come easily in our society, that, in fact, our worth as persons is often measured by what we accomplish or who we please. Perhaps we recognize that the self we need to navigate the world can be hard to come by, and that many consequential decisions will depend on it. Perhaps, taking stock of our society, we share the worry that our kids are too self-focused, but then, based on the same reflection, tell them they’re special.

item.title: Peer Support May Be the Answer to the Mental Health Crisis
item.description:
Psychology

Peer Support May Be the Answer to the Mental Health Crisis

Selecting and training peers unlocks new possibilities in care.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • There are insufficient mental health resources available to respond to today's mental health crisis.
  • Peer support is a validated and consensus-recommended way to extend psychological support.
  • Effective peer support requires both shared experiences and key personal qualities like empathy.
Source: ninosousa/Pixabay

In previous books and papers, I’ve asserted that a tectonic shift in the delivery of mental health services is required, especially in the delivery of psychological support during and in the wake of crises and disasters (Everly, 2020, 2023; Everly and Lating, 2026). The key to constructive change resides in change predicated upon retention, recollection, and introspection. Those who fail to remember the past are condemned to repeat it, noted Santayana. Residing within that condemnation is an elusive maturity that will forever evade those who fail to heed the warning. They will be trapped in a perpetual infancy. And while it is true that those who fail to study the past are doomed to repeat it, those who fail to shape the future are condemned to endure a future shaped by others, as Toffler noted.

The Crisis

The interested observer cannot help but be struck by the canyon-like vitriolic schisms existing within political, economic, and educational spheres. Loneliness, anxiety, depression, and a sense of isolation seem pervasive, ironically, in an age of ubiquitous social media. Much to the dismay of many, there appears to be a debate concerning the value of free speech itself. The interested reader would prosper from insights provided by two brilliant summaries: A Nation of Wimps: The High Cost of Invasive Parenting by Hara Estroff Marano and The Coddling of the American Mind by Jonathan Haidt and Greg Lukianoff. As we struggle to resolve these challenges, it is important to remember the value of open communication and psychological support.

Practitioners within the fields of psychology, psychiatry, social work, and counseling have much to offer in the provision of psychological support, especially when properly trained in crisis intervention and disaster response. But the harsh reality is that there exists a shortage of mental health practitioners, according to the American Psychological Association, the American Psychiatric Association, and the World Health Organization. Those shortages will be compounded by the realization that not all clinicians are culturally competent, trauma-informed, and crisis intervention trained. Finally, there remains a stigma surrounding seeking formal mental health services.

Peer Support as a Force Multiplier

In addition to the American Psychiatric Association and the World Health Organization, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) has embraced the use of peer support personnel (SAMHSA,2015, 2023, 2024) to provide psychological support.

Peers are those who share some significant life experience with those they assist. Shared experiences could be occupational, cultural, geographic, economic, or even health-related challenges, to name but a few. For example, peer support has been used within the military, emergency services, healthcare settings for both staff and patients, and community crisis response and disaster mental health services. Cherie Castellano’s award-winning papers and peer programs have revealed the potential of peer support across many applications. Research has documented the ability of peers to deliver effective psychological support predicated upon specialized training (see Everly and Lating, 2026, for a review). This begs the question, "How do we effectively mobilize these peer resources?"

Selecting Peer Support Interventionists: 7 Qualities

The first step is recruiting peer support team members. Rather than relying upon good intentions and shared life experiences alone, the following personal qualities have been recommended in the selection of peer team members:

  1. Stability within shared life experiences that can be used as a solid foundation for assisting others
  2. Empathy without loss of objectivity
  3. Humility without low self-esteem or self-erasure (minimization)
  4. Confidence without arrogance
  5. Hopefulness without dismissiveness
  6. Reliability without rigidity
  7. Openness to learning and supervision

10 Competencies of a Peer Support Interventionist

Expertise gained by good intentions and experience alone will prove insufficient. After the selection process is complete, specialized training must be pursued. Here are 10 competencies that peer training should help create:

  1. Formation of trusting cooperative peer relationships without losing a sense of boundaries
  2. Collaboration with other providers, especially licensed healthcare providers
  3. Communication that is open without interrupting or rushing to “fix” problems
  4. De-escalation of acute intrusive cognitive ruminations or emotional arousal
  5. Basic problem-solving proficiency
  6. Delivery of psychological first aid (PFA)
  7. Cultivation of tailored empowerment and self-efficacy
  8. Identification and coordination of resources
  9. Awareness of one's own limitations
  10. Management and monitoring of one's own countertransference

Mobilizing the power of peers residing within every organization and community may not only be a way to mitigate crises and disasters, but also a way to foster civility and promote increased social cohesion.

(C) 2026, George S. Everly, Jr., PhD

item.title: Developing Self-Trust
item.description:
Confidence

Developing Self-Trust

Exploring honesty and kindness as the roots of self-reliance.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • True self-trust combines honesty with yourself and consistent self-kindness.
  • Self-examination with compassion makes it safer to face personal truths and shadows.
  • Allowing curiosity and “unknowing” fosters deeper self-understanding and openness to others.
Source: Alexander Aguero/Unsplash

We don’t talk much about trusting ourselves. And when we do, it’s not easy to understand what we’re talking about. Discussions about trust are typically about what happens between two or more people. We seem to approach the idea of trusting ourselves when we speak of someone being confident. Coincidentally, the Latin root of the word confidence means “with trust.” However, the common description of someone as confident suggests the person acts boldly with audacity. Such an understanding loses the depth of what it means to truly trust ourselves.

Two Beliefs

During the Human Potential movement, there was growing interest in what it meant to trust someone. The experiments involving trust used the following operational definition: I trust you if I hold two beliefs about you: that you will tell me the truth and that you will be kind to me. I’ve applied this definition of trust both in my personal and professional relationships. I decided, why not use the same definition of trust when referring to trusting myself? Hence, I trust myself when I believe I will tell myself the truth, and I’ll be kind to myself.

The Truth About Me

Let’s look at what it takes to believe we will allow ourselves to see the truth about ourselves.

  • Self-examination. Being committed to living a self-examining life makes it more likely that we will come to some truths about ourselves.
  • Compassion. The more we hold compassion for what we see about ourselves, the more likely we are to continue looking.
  • Curious about shadow material. Shadow material is that part of us we deem unacceptable and relegate to the unconscious. There’s a tendency to project these parts of ourselves onto other people. That is, we see in them what we deny about ourselves. The more strongly we react emotionally to someone, the more likely we are to see our shadow in that person. Some common projections include insensitivity, self-centeredness, irresponsibility, pretentiousness, and non-cooperation.
  • Get help. A useful strategy is to get help from those we trust or from a professional. Their feedback can illuminate our blind spots.

Knowing Our Truth About People, Places, and Things

We’re not going to know the absolute truth about people, places, and things. However, we can strengthen our belief that we will allow ourselves to know these things. Here are some helpful aids.

  • Allow for unknowing. Certainty tends to close an inquiry. Unknowing allows for more exploration.
  • Remain curious. This is especially important with people. It’s only too easy to decide who they are when we need them to be a certain way.
  • Listen to diverse perspectives. This allows us to take on different points of view, freeing us from rigidly holding down one position. It can help to track a sense of urgency that can arise in the chest when hearing something directly opposed to our beliefs. Take a breath and see if you can return to listening without having to challenge, correct, or advise.
  • Remain an apprentice. Avoid seeing yourself as an expert, even though it might sell. Claiming expertise can be a serious hindrance to learning.
article continues after advertisement

Believing We Will Be Kind to Ourselves

It should be obvious that it’s difficult to trust those who are unkind to us. We face the same predicament when we are unkind to ourselves. Let’s look at what might limit our cruelty toward ourselves.

  • Track unkindness. This is the starting place. Let yourself notice critical thoughts, a lack of self-forgiveness, neglecting basic needs for rest, food, exercise, and companionship, and compulsive or addictive behaviors.
  • Interrupt cruelty. Make the commitment to identify one way you treat yourself cruelly. You may discover that the cruelty has an underlying motive, such as “I’ll be a better person if I punish myself for this mistake” or “Being unkind to myself like my parents were, allows me to stay attached to them.” There can be a variety of reasons why cruelty allegedly makes sense.
  • Confide in someone. It helps to make your commitment to kindness talkable. Decide if you can hold yourself shamelessly accountable for your acts of cruelty with a friend.

A commitment to self-trust is a psycho-spiritual practice. It’s a decision to live with more compassion and get right with ourselves. How we treat ourselves often results in how we treat others. If you stay with the practice, you’ll see how trusting yourself can lead to a greater willingness to take risks, act more authentically, be more curious, and give and receive love with more ease.

item.title: The Two Sides of Music Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

The Two Sides of Music Therapy

Music healing is historic; its role in brain rehab is evolving.

Posted June 28, 2026

Key points
  • Music therapy is the evidence-based use of music in a clinical setting to accomplish therapeutic goals.
  • Neurological and social consequences of a brain injury can be addressed with music therapy.
  • It is important to keep in mind cultural influences and potential harm when exercising music therapy.
Music Therapy Session
Source: Adobe Stock

By Prav Prathapan, Encephalitis International

The use of music for healing has been understood since time immemorial. By 5000 BC, music was already used for healing by Egyptian priest-physicians.1 In the ancient West, Apollo was the Greek god of both music and medicine, while his son Aesculapius was said to cure diseases of the mind by using song and music.

Fast forward to today, and music is used all around the world to address recovery from an acquired brain injury (ABI), irrespective of its causes—an inflammation (encephalitis), trauma, or other medical events (stroke, meningitis). "Music therapy," as it is formally known, is the evidence-based practice that uses music to work on functional goals. It is provided by music therapists who are usually trained musicians themselves and have completed an accredited music therapy programme.

There are two basic types of music therapy: receptive and active (also known as expressive). The former guides patients in listening or responding to music, and the latter engages patients in the act of making music. Listening to music can improve heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure.

Benefits for people recovering from a brain injury

“Caring for someone with a brain injury is far from easy. But the simple things in life—music, nature, food, laughter, family and friends—can bring solace and happiness to us all.”—Catherine Jessop, who cares for her husband Alan, diagnosed with autoimmune encephalitis in 2016

Due to its brain-stimulating properties, music therapy can be used with individuals with ABI to improve speech/language and motor skills. Consequences of a brain injury include dysarthria: a motor speech disorder where damage to the nervous system causes muscles that produce speech to become paralysed or weakened; and aphasia (also known as dysphasia): an impairment in a person’s ability to comprehend or formulate language because of dysfunction in specific brain regions.

Singing training is a form of neurorehabilitation that can improve speech clarity and coordination of speech muscles. Melodic intonation therapy (MIT), for example, is the practice of communicating with others by singing, which can promote socialisation in addition to improving speech.2 It was developed in 1973 to help people with communication disorders caused by damage to the left hemisphere of the brain by purportedly engaging language-capable regions in the undamaged right hemisphere. Changes to memory are often a significant consequence of ABI and can be addressed with music therapy, with the use of familiar songs as retrieval cues being well-documented.3

article continues after advertisement

Rhyming, chanting, and clapping can help develop concentration and promote cognitive development, with studies showing that easily distracted patients are able to focus on a song for a significant length of time. Songwriting is a similar tool that is used to help in this regard. By performing music with the therapist or other people, patients’ mood and emotions can be significantly improved, and anxiety can be lowered. This is particularly important as depression and anxiety are frequent consequences of a brain injury.4

Limits of music therapy

In many countries, including the United States, music therapists do not diagnose, so diagnosing mental disorders would not be within the scope of practice. On the other hand, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) in the United Kingdom has claimed that music therapy is an effective method in helping people with mental health issues, and more should be done to offer this type of treatment.

In some countries, an individual may have multiple cultural identities that may be different from those of the music therapists. These include race, ethnicity, culture, and/or heritage, religion, sex, ability/disability, education, and socioeconomic status. It is therefore important to integrate multicultural therapy with music therapy consistent with the life experiences and cultural values of clients, rather than basing therapy on the therapist’s worldview or the dominant culture’s norms.

Finally, it is important to keep in mind that some music may cause harm. For example, autoimmune encephalitis (brain inflammation caused by the body’s immune system) has been recently included among many possible aetiologies of musicogenic epilepsy based on reports of music-induced seizures in patients with anti-GAD65 autoimmune encephalitis.5 This further highlights the need for care and individualisation when delivering such therapy to patients.

Conclusion

Music therapy offers a powerful, evidence-based avenue for supporting recovery from ABIs such as those post-encephalitis, addressing not only the neurological consequences of the condition but its broader emotional and social impacts. When delivered thoughtfully and tailored to the individual, music therapy holds promise as a complementary tool in the journey of recovery.
